A.title: Getting Ready Lesson A · Introduction to sounds
A.tag: Sounds, the sound wall and pre-writing strokes
notes: Getting Ready lessons introduce the 44 phonemes and letter formation. None of the content is expected to be mastered - the core lessons will review it.

intro: Words are made of sounds. Today we will listen for the sounds in words and learn how our mouth makes them. Our sound wall shows a mouth picture and a key word for each sound.

Some sounds can be stretched out (continuous sounds like /mmm/ and /sss/). Some sounds are quick (stop sounds like /p/). Some sounds turn the voice on (feel your throat hum for /m/); others are quiet (/s/, /p/).
Introduce the routine hand gestures: stretch hands apart for a continuous sound, chop for a stop sound, touch the throat for a voiced sound.
sounds: mouth open wide, voice on, vowel
lips together, quiet puff, stop sound

strokes: Sky writing and tracing: big arm movements in the air, then trace shapes with a finger.
Circles: start at the top, go around to the left (anticlockwise) and back to the top.
Curves: half circle, smile and hump strokes - the building blocks of many letters (c, o, u, n, m).

B.title: Getting Ready Lesson B · Consonants: place of articulation
B.tag: Where in the mouth each consonant sound is made

intro: Consonant sounds are made by blocking or squeezing the air somewhere in the mouth. Today we will find out WHERE each sound is made. The sound wall groups consonants by the place in the mouth.

Say each sound and feel it: /p/ /b/ /m/ use the lips together. /f/ /v/ put the teeth on the lip. /th/ puts the tongue between the teeth. /t/ /d/ /n/ /s/ /z/ put the tongue behind the top teeth. /sh/ /ch/ /j/ /y/ /r/ lift the tongue. /k/ /g/ /ŋ/ /w/ pull the tongue back. /h/ comes from the back of the throat.
sounds: sheep, treasure, chicken, jar, yellow, red

strokes: Vertical lines: start at the top and pull straight down.
Horizontal lines: start on the left and go across to the right.
Slanted lines: down to the right (\) and down to the left (/).

C.concept: Consonants: manner of articulation (stops and nasals)
C.title: Getting Ready Lesson C · Consonants: manner of articulation (stops and nasals)
C.tag: How the air is stopped or sent through the nose

intro: Yesterday we learned WHERE sounds are made. Today we learn HOW the air moves. Stop sounds stop the air completely and then let it pop out: /p/ /b/ /t/ /d/ /k/ /g/. They are quick - do not add /uh/.
Nasal sounds send the air out through the nose: /m/ /n/ /ŋ/. Hold your nose and try to say /mmm/ - you can't! Nasal sounds can be stretched out.
sounds: stop sounds with the lips; /p/ quiet, /b/ voice on
stop sounds with the tongue behind the teeth; /t/ quiet, /d/ voice on
stop sounds with the tongue pulled back; /k/ quiet, /g/ voice on
nasal: lips together, air through the nose
nasal: tongue behind top teeth, air through the nose
nasal: tongue pulled back, air through the nose

strokes: Uppercase L: pull down, then across to the right.
Uppercase F: pull down, across at the top, across in the middle.
Uppercase E: pull down, across at the top, middle and bottom.

D.title: Getting Ready Lesson D · Consonants: fricatives and affricates
D.tag: Sounds made by squeezing the air

intro: Fricative sounds squeeze the air through a small space so it makes friction - a hissing or buzzing: /f/ /v/ /th/ /s/ /z/ /sh/ /zh/ /h/. Rub your thumb and finger together for the friction gesture. These sounds can be stretched out.
Affricate sounds start like a stop and end like a fricative: /ch/ and /j/. They are quick. Each pair has a quiet sound and a voiced sound - feel your throat.
sounds: fricative: teeth on lip; /f/ quiet, /v/ voice on
fricative: tongue between teeth; quiet / voice on
fricative: teeth together; /s/ quiet, /z/ voice on
fricative: lips round, tongue back; /sh/ quiet, /zh/ voice on
fricative from the back of the throat, quiet
affricate: a stop then a squeeze; /ch/ quiet, /j/ voice on

strokes: Uppercase H: two lines down, then across the middle.
Uppercase T: across the top, then down the middle.
Uppercase I: down, then a short line across the top and bottom.

E.title: Getting Ready Lesson E · Consonants: glides and liquids
E.tag: Sounds where the tongue moves smoothly

intro: Glide and liquid sounds do not block the air much - the tongue comes close but the air flows freely. /y/ and /w/ are glides: the mouth glides into the next vowel. /l/ and /r/ are liquids. All four have the voice on.
Practise saying /y/ and /w/ before vowels: /yă/, /wă/. Say /l/ and /r/ without adding /uh/: /lll/, /rrr/.
sounds: liquid: tongue behind top teeth, voice flows around the sides
liquid: tongue lifted and pulled back a little, voice on

strokes: Uppercase O: start at the top and go around to the left.
Uppercase Q: like O, then add a short tail.
Uppercase C: start at the top, curve around to the left and stop.
Uppercase G: like C, then across and down.

F.concept: Consonant review: place, manner and voice
F.title: Getting Ready Lesson F · Consonant review: place, manner and voice

intro: We review all the consonant sounds on the sound wall. For each sound: where is it made (place)? how does the air move (manner)? is the voice on or off? Use the hand gestures.
Play 'find the sound': say a word, students find the sound wall card for the first sound.
sounds: lips together / teeth on lip / tongue between teeth / tongue behind teeth / tongue lifted / tongue pulled back / back of throat
stops, nasals, fricatives, affricates, glides and liquids

strokes: Uppercase U: down, curve, up.
Uppercase J: down, curve to the left.
Uppercase S: curve to the left, then to the right, like a snake.

G.title: Getting Ready Lesson G · Introduction to vowels
G.tag: Consonants block the air; vowels let it flow

intro: There are two kinds of sounds. Consonant sounds block or squeeze the air somewhere in the mouth. Vowel sounds let the air flow out freely with the voice on - the mouth is open. Every word and every syllable has a vowel sound.
Say each sound and decide: consonant or vowel? /fff/ - the air is squeezed: consonant. /ăăă/ - the air flows: vowel.
sounds: vowel: air flows freely, voice on
vowel: air flows, mouth a little open

strokes: Uppercase D: down, then a big curve from the top back to the bottom.
Uppercase P: down, then a small curve at the top.
Uppercase B: down, then two curves.
Uppercase R: down, a small curve at the top, then a slanted line down.

H.title: Getting Ready Lesson H · Vowels: the vowel valley
H.tag: Vowel sounds ordered by how open the mouth is

intro: The vowel valley shows the vowel sounds in order. On the left side the mouth starts almost closed with a smile (/ē/) and opens wider and wider (/ĭ/, /ā/, /ĕ/, /ă/). At the bottom of the valley the mouth is wide open (/ī/, /ŭ/, /ŏ/). Going up the right side the lips get rounder and rounder (/ō/, /oo/, /yū/, /ū/).
Say the vowels in order and feel your mouth open and then round: /ē/ /ĭ/ /ā/ /ĕ/ /ă/ /ī/ /ŭ/ /ŏ/ /ō/ /oo/ /yū/ /ū/.
sounds: wide open then glide to a smile

strokes: Uppercase K: down, then two slanted lines meeting in the middle.
Uppercase M: down, slant down, slant up, down.
Uppercase N: down, slant down, up.
Uppercase A: slant down to the left, slant down to the right, across the middle.

I.concept: Vowels: schwa, diphthongs and r-controlled vowels
I.title: Getting Ready Lesson I · Vowels: schwa, diphthongs and r-controlled vowels

intro: Some vowel sounds are special. The schwa /ə/ is the quick, relaxed vowel in unstressed syllables (the first sound in above). We do not stretch it.
Diphthongs are two vowel sounds that glide together so fast we hear one sound: /oi/ (oil) and /ow/ (owl). Feel your mouth move.
R-controlled vowels are vowel sounds changed by R: /ar/ (arm), /er/ (earth), /or/ (orange). In our accent we do not say the /r/ at the end.
sounds: r-controlled: mouth a little open, tongue pulled back

strokes: Uppercase V: slant down to the right, slant up to the right.
Uppercase W: down, up, down, up.
Uppercase X: slant down to the right, then slant down to the left.

J.concept: Sound wall review: consonants and vowels
J.title: Getting Ready Lesson J · Sound wall review: consonants and vowels

intro: We review the whole sound wall. Say each sound with its key word and mouth picture. Sort sounds: consonant or vowel? voiced or unvoiced? stop or continuous?
Play 'I spy a sound': give a sound; students find it on the wall and say a word that starts with it.
sounds: review by place, manner and voice
review the vowel valley, schwa, diphthongs and r-controlled vowels

strokes: Uppercase Y: two slanted lines meeting in the middle, then down.
Uppercase Z: across, slant down to the left, across.

1.title: Lesson 1 a /ă/
notes: This is the first core lesson. Only Steps 1, 5 and 7 are used. Steps 2-4 begin once a few graphemes are known.
Use the sound wall mouth picture for /ă/ (apple). Watch for the /ă/ sound in cat (Australian/NZ short a).
intro: Today we are learning about the letter A. A is a vowel. The letter A spells the /ă/ sound like at the beginning of apple.
A can come at the beginning of a word, such as at and as. A can also come in the middle of a word, such as cat and map.
1.gesture: To make the /ă/ sound as in 'apple', open your mouth wide like this... (model). Be sure your voice is on. Like all vowels, /ă/ is a continuous sound that can be stretched out (use continuous hand motion). Watch me /ăăă/. You try /ăăă/.
1.soundwall: Add 'a' under /ă/ on the vowel valley.
1.formation: Practise letter formation for uppercase A and lowercase a (see the letter formation animations in the slides).
1.irr_teach_note: the: TH has not been introduced yet; E spells /ŭ/ (or /ē/ before a vowel). Learn the word 'by heart'.

5.title: Lesson 5 VC & CVC Words

bd.chain: at → mat → sat → Sam → am → at

intro: We have learned four letters and their sounds: a, m, s, t. Today we will use them to read and spell words. Some words have a vowel and a consonant (VC), like at. Some words have a consonant, a vowel and a consonant (CVC), like mat.
To read a word, we say each sound and then blend the sounds together: /mmmăăăt/, mat. To spell a word, we say the word, count the sounds, and write a letter for each sound.

42.title: Lesson 42 FLSZ Spelling Rule
42.tag: FLSZ spelling rule: ff, ll, ss, zz
notes: The FLSZ rule: when a one-syllable word has a short vowel followed by /f/, /l/, /s/ or /z/ at the end, the final letter is doubled (off, hill, miss, buzz). The doubled letter spells one sound.
Word work today uses writing, because most manipulative letter sets have only one of each letter.

bd.chain: hill → fill → fell → tell → bell → bill → will → well → yell → sell → smell → spell → spill → still

intro: Today we are learning a spelling rule. When a short word has a short vowel and ends with the sound /f/, /l/, /s/ or /z/, we usually double the last letter: off, hill, miss, buzz.
The two letters spell one sound. When you read, say the sound once: /ŏf/, off. When you spell, remember the rule: FLSZ - f, l, s and z are doubled after a short vowel at the end of a word.
Remember that some words are exceptions, such as bus, gas, yes and if.

43.title: Lesson 43 -all, -oll, -ull

45.title: Lesson 45 sh /sh/
notes: Although students have learned double letters and CK, SH is the first grapheme that represents a sound that is different from either of its letters.

bd.chain: ship → shop → shot → shut → shun → shin → chin* → thin* →
bd.note: Use: ship → shop → shot → shut → shun → shin → shed → shell → shall → sham → slam → slash → flash → fish → dish → wish

intro: A consonant digraph is when two consonants come together to make one sound. You have already learned about a consonant digraph. We have talked about CK. When C and K are together at the end of a word, they make one sound, /k/.
The two consonants S and H have their own sounds, /s/ and /h/. But when these consonants come together in words, they make one new sound, /sh/, like at the beginning of the word sheep.
The consonant digraph SH can come at the beginning of a word, such as ship and shop. The consonant digraph SH can come at the end of a word, such as fish and wish.

54.title: Lesson 54 a_e /ā/
notes: VCe = vowel, consonant, silent e. The silent e signals that the vowel says its long sound (its name). Teach the pattern by changing short-vowel words: cap → cape, mad → made.
Word work uses writing or magnetic letters with a separate e tile.

bd.chain: mad → made → mate → male → sale → same → came → cane → cape → tape → take → bake → lake → late → gate

intro: We have learned that the letter A spells /ă/ as in cat. Today we will learn that A can also spell /ā/, the long A sound, which is the letter's name.

Look at this word: cap. Now I add an e at the end: cape. The e at the end is silent, but it does a job: it tells the vowel to say its name. A, consonant, silent e - we call this the VCe pattern. c-a-p-e, cape. The vowel says /ā/.
When you read a word with a vowel, one consonant and an e at the end, the vowel is long: made, same, take. When you spell, remember the silent e at the end.

64.title: Lesson 64 -ed
notes: -ed makes a verb past tense. It spells three sounds: /t/ after quiet sounds (jumped), /d/ after voiced sounds (called), /əd/ after t or d (rested, landed). Students spell -ed for all three.
Today's words are base words that do not change spelling. The doubling rule (stop → stopped) and drop-e rule come in Lessons 107 and 109.

bd.chain: jump → jumped → bumped → dumped → dusted → rusted → rested → tested → nested → melted → yelled → filled → called

intro: Today we will learn the suffix -ed. When we add -ed to an action word (a verb), it means the action already happened - in the past. Today I jump. Yesterday I jumped.
-ed can sound three ways. After quiet sounds it says /t/: jumped, asked. After noisy sounds it says /d/: yelled, called. After /t/ or /d/ it says /əd/ and adds a syllable: rested, handed.
No matter how it sounds, we spell it e-d. When you read a word that ends in -ed, cover the -ed, read the base word, then add the ending.

66.title: Lesson 66 Closed & Open Syllables
notes: A syllable is a word or word part with one vowel sound. A closed syllable ends in a consonant and the vowel is short (hop, kick). An open syllable ends in a vowel and the vowel is long - it says its name (go, hi, me, we, she).
This lesson makes he, be, me, we, she, go, no, so decodable.

bd.chain: be → bet → met → me → we → wet → set → so → no → not → hot → ho* → go → got

intro: A syllable is a word or part of a word with one vowel sound. Clap the syllables: cat (1), rabbit (2), banana (3).
A closed syllable has a vowel followed by at least one consonant. The consonant 'closes in' the vowel, and the vowel is short: hop, kick, just. All the CVC words we know are closed syllables.
An open syllable ends with the vowel. Nothing closes it in, so the vowel is long - it says its name: go, hi, me, we, she, so, no. Say the sounds: /g/ /ō/, go.
Knowing whether a syllable is open or closed helps us read the vowel.

68.title: Lesson 68 Open/Closed
notes: When one consonant sits between two vowels (V/CV), divide before the consonant: ro-bot, o-pen. The first syllable is open, so its vowel is long. If that does not make a real word, try dividing after the consonant (closed, short vowel): rob-in, cab-in. This flexibility is called 'set for variability'.

bd.chain: robot → robin → rob → ro → rodent → basin → basic → bacon → begin → began → be → being → unit → unite

intro: Yesterday we divided words between two consonants (rab/bit). Today we will look at words with only one consonant between the vowels, like robot: r-o-b-o-t.

When there is one consonant in the middle, we usually divide before the consonant: ro / bot. The first syllable is open, so the vowel says its name: /rō/. Then read the second syllable: /bŏt/. Blend: robot.

Sometimes dividing before the consonant does not make a real word. Then be flexible: try dividing after the consonant and make the vowel short: rob / in, robin. Try the long sound first, then the short sound.

69.title: Lesson 69 tch /ch/
notes: Use TCH right after a short vowel at the end of a word (catch, itch). Use CH after a consonant or a long vowel (bench, much, coach). Exceptions: much, such, rich, which, sandwich.

bd.chain: match → batch → patch → latch → hatch → hutch → Dutch → ditch → pitch → witch → switch → stitch → stretch → fetch → sketch

intro: We know that CH spells /ch/ as in chip and much. Today we will learn another way to spell /ch/: TCH. T-C-H spells one sound, /ch/, like at the end of catch.

TCH comes at the end of a word right after a short vowel: match, fetch, itch, witch. After a consonant we use CH: bench, lunch. This is like CK: right after a short vowel we use ck (back), and after a consonant we use k (milk).

72.title: Lesson 72 Long VCC

75.title: Lesson 75 -le
notes: -le is a final stable syllable: consonant + le at the end of a word (ap-ple, puz-zle). Divide before the consonant that comes before -le. If the first syllable is closed, the vowel is short (lit-tle); if open, it is long (ta-ble).

bd.chain: puddle → paddle → saddle → riddle → middle → little → battle → rattle → cattle → settle → kettle → nettle

intro: A syllable is a word or word part with one vowel sound. We know closed syllables (short vowel) and open syllables (long vowel). Today we will learn a final stable syllable: -le.

Final means it comes last. Stable means it always looks and sounds the same. -le comes at the end of a word with a consonant in front of it: ap-ple, puz-zle. The -le syllable says /əl/ - the e is silent and the L makes the sound.
To read a word ending in -le, divide before the consonant that comes before -le: lit / tle, ta / ble. Read the first syllable, then add the -le syllable.

notes: This lesson has been added into the Australian scope and sequence because ER commonly represents the sound /ə/ at the end of many two-syllable words (letter, number, sister).
Word work today uses writing because of the double letters.

bd.chain: bath → baths → paths → path → pat → past → mast → fast → cast → last → blast → blass → brass → grass → glass → class

intro: We have been learning that the /er/ sound is an r-controlled vowel sound. ER can come in the middle of a word, such as the words verb and fern. ER can also come at the end of a word, such as the word her.
However, when we see ER at the end of a two-syllable word, it is usually pronounced using the schwa sound, /ə/, such as the words letter and number.
80AUS.gesture: To make the schwa /ə/ sound, open your mouth just a little bit, like this... (model). Be sure your voice is on. Unlike all the other vowel sounds, we don't really stretch out the schwa. We say it more quickly. Watch me /ə/. You try /ə/. Sometimes, a schwa can sound a little like a short u /ŭ/ or a short i /ĭ/, but it's actually more relaxed than either of those. Watch me again /ə/. You try again /ə/.

81.title: Lesson 81 ir, ur /er/

notes: IR and UR spell the same sound as ER: /er/. IR is usually in the middle of a word (bird, girl, first). UR can be in the middle (turn, hurt) or at the end (fur, blur). Spelling /er/ requires remembering the word - see Lesson 82.

intro: We learned that ER spells /er/, as in her and fern. Today we will learn two more spellings for the same sound. IR spells /er/, like in bird and girl. UR spells /er/, like in turn and hurt.

82.tag: Spelling /er/: er, ir, ur, w + or
notes: /er/ has several spellings: er, ir, ur, and or after w (work, word, world). When spelling, use these hints: er is the most common and is used at the end of two-syllable words; ur/ir are common in one-syllable words; after w, /er/ is often spelled or.

84.title: Lesson 84 ai, ay/ā/
84.tag: The vowel teams AI and AY spell /ā/
notes: A vowel team is two or more letters that work together to spell one vowel sound. AI spells /ā/ at the beginning or in the middle of a word (aim, rain). AY spells /ā/ at the end of a word or syllable (day, playing).
We now have four spellings of /ā/: a (open syllable), a_e, ai, ay.

bd.chain: rain → main → pain → paint → saint → sail → mail → tail → trail → train → brain → drain → day → play → clay → stay → tray

intro: A vowel team is two or more letters that work together to make one sound. We have already learned some ways to spell /ā/: a in an open syllable (baby) and a_e (cake). Today we will learn two vowel teams that spell /ā/.
AI spells /ā/ like in rain. AI comes at the beginning or in the middle of a word: aim, wait, paint. AY also spells /ā/ like in day. AY comes at the end of a word: say, play, stay.
When you hear /ā/ at the end of a word, use AY. In the middle, use AI or a_e.

85.title: Lesson 85 ee, ea, ey /ē/
85.tag: The vowel teams EE, EA and EY spell /ē/
notes: EE and EA spell /ē/ at the beginning, middle or end of a word (eel, feet, see; eat, team, sea). EY spells /ē/ at the end of a word, often in two-syllable words (key, monkey, turkey).
EA also spells /ĕ/ (head) and /ā/ (great) - Lessons 94 and 114.

bd.chain: see → seed → feed → feet → meet → meat → beat → bead → read → lead → leaf → leap → keep → deep → sleep → sweep → sweet

intro: We know that /ē/ can be spelled e in an open syllable (be, began) and e_e (these). Today we will learn three vowel teams that spell /ē/.

EE spells /ē/ like in feet and see. EA spells /ē/ like in eat and team. Both can come at the beginning, middle or end of a word. EY spells /ē/ at the end of a word, like key and monkey. It is often at the end of a two-syllable word: mon-key, tur-key.
When you spell /ē/ in the middle of a word, it could be ee or ea - you have to remember which.

86.title: Lesson 86 oa, ow, oe /ō/

notes: OA spells /ō/ at the beginning or middle of a word (oat, boat). OW spells /ō/ at the end of a word or syllable (show, grow, yellow) - OW also spells /ow/ (cow), Lesson 96. OE spells /ō/ at the end of a few words (toe, doe, goes).

88.title: Lesson 88 Vowel Teams Review 1
88.tag: Vowel teams review 1: ai, ay, ee, ea, ey, oa, ow, oe, ie, igh

notes: EW spells /ū/ at the end of a word (new, blew, flew). UI spells /ū/ in the middle of a word (fruit, suit, juice). UE spells /ū/ at the end of a word (blue, glue, true). EW and UE also spell /yū/ (few, cue) - Lesson 115.

notes: In Australian/NZ English, the sound in saw, haul and caught is the same as the /or/ in fork and more. The UFLI US edition calls it /aw/. AU comes in the middle of a word (haul, sauce); AW at the end of a word or before n/l (saw, lawn, crawl); AUGH before t (caught, taught).

95.title: Lesson 95 oi, oy /oi/
95.tag: The diphthongs OI and OY spell /oi/
notes: A diphthong is a vowel sound that glides from one sound to another (/oi/ = /o/ gliding to /i/). OI spells /oi/ in the middle of a word (coin, point). OY spells /oi/ at the end of a word or syllable (toy, enjoy, royal).

bd.chain: oil → boil → coil → coin → join → joint → point → moist → hoist → foil → soil → spoil → boy → toy → joy → enjoy → ploy

intro: Today we will learn a new vowel sound, /oi/, like in oil and boy. It is a diphthong: two vowel sounds that glide together so fast we say them as one - /o/ /i/, /oi/.

99.title: Lesson 99 -s/-es
notes: This lesson revisits -s and -es as morphemes: word parts that change meaning. -s/-es make nouns plural (one dog, two dogs) and change verbs (I run, he runs). Use -es after s, x, z, sh, ch.

bd.chain: class → classes → glasses → grasses → grass → gross → grows → glows → glow → blow → blows → brushes → brush → crush → crushes

intro: A morpheme is a word part that changes a word's meaning. A suffix is a morpheme added to the end of a word. We know the suffixes -s and -es.

Nouns are people, animals, places and things: dog, shirt, box. Adding -s or -es makes a noun mean more than one: dogs, shirts, boxes. Verbs describe an action: run, brush. Adding -s or -es changes the verb: I run, she runs; I brush, he brushes.
Add -es after s, x, z, sh and ch, because -es adds a syllable that we can hear: box-es, brush-es.

107.title: Lesson 107 Doubling Rule -ed, -ing
notes: When a one-syllable word has one vowel followed by one consonant (a 1-1-1 word: hop, stop, run), double the final consonant before adding a suffix that starts with a vowel (-ed, -ing): hop → hopped, hopping. Doubling keeps the vowel short (hop-ping vs. ho-ping).
Do not double when the word ends in two consonants (jump → jumping) or has a vowel team (rain → rained).

bd.chain: hop → hopped → hopping → shopping → shopped → stopped → stopping → dropping → dropped → drop → drip → dripping → dripped

intro: We know the suffixes -ed and -ing. Today we will learn a spelling rule for adding them. Look at the word stop: s-t-o-p. It has one vowel, then one consonant at the end. We call this a 1-1-1 word: one syllable, one vowel, one final consonant.

When we add -ed or -ing to a 1-1-1 word, we double the last consonant: stop → stopped, stopping. Why? The double consonant keeps the vowel short. If we wrote 'stoping', the o would look long (sto-ping).
If the word ends in two consonants (jump) or has two vowels (rain), do not double: jumped, raining.

“What made your day so busy?” he asked. Edwin explained.

“It started this morning when I dropped off some letters at the post office. The line was so long that I ended up running late for work. Then, at work, I had so many meetings. It felt like they were never going to end. I planned to come home for lunch, but I was so busy I skipped that trip.

notes: The same 1-1-1 doubling rule applies to -er and -est: big → bigger, biggest; hot → hotter, hottest. Do not double after two consonants or a vowel team (fast → faster; cool → cooler).

If the word ends in two consonants or has a vowel team, do not double: fast → faster, fastest; cool → cooler, coolest.

109.title: Lesson 109 Drop -e Rule
notes: When a word ends in silent e, drop the e before adding a suffix that begins with a vowel (-ed, -ing, -er, -est): hope → hoped, hoping; nice → nicer, nicest. Keep the e before a suffix that begins with a consonant (hopeful, safely).

bd.chain: hope → hoped → hoping → hopping* → bake → baked → baking → baker → brave → braver → bravest → cute → cuter → cutest → smile → smiled → smiling

intro: We have learned the doubling rule. Today we will learn another spelling rule for adding suffixes: the drop -e rule.

Look at the word hope: it ends in silent e. When we add a suffix that starts with a vowel, like -ing, -ed, -er or -est, we drop the silent e first: hope → hoping, hoped. Nice → nicer, nicest. Bake → baked, baking, baker.
We drop the e because the suffix's vowel now does the silent e's job of keeping the vowel long: ho-ping. If the suffix starts with a consonant, keep the e: hopeful, safely, nicely.

110.title: Lesson 110 -y to i Rule
notes: When a word ends in a consonant + y, change the y to i before adding a suffix (-er, -est, -ed, -es): happy → happier, happiest; cry → cried, cries; puppy → puppies. Do not change y before -ing (crying) or when a vowel comes before y (play → played).

bd.chain: cry → cried → cries → crying → try → tried → tries → trying → happy → happier → happiest → happily → puppy → puppies → candy → candies

intro: We have learned the doubling rule and the drop -e rule. Today we will learn one more spelling rule: the y to i rule.
Look at happy: it ends in a consonant and then y. When we add a suffix like -er, -est, -ed or -es, we change the y to i: happy → happier, happiest. Cry → cried, cries. Puppy → puppies.
We do not change the y before -ing, because we do not want two i's together: crying, hurrying. And if a vowel comes before the y, just add the suffix: play → played, plays.

111.title: Lesson 111 -ar, -or /ə/

notes: In an unstressed final syllable, AR and OR are pronounced with the schwa /ə/ (the same sound as ER in letter): dollar, doctor. In Australian/NZ English these endings all sound like /ə/. Spelling requires memory: ar (dollar, collar, sugar), or (doctor, actor, visitor).

notes: Low-frequency spellings of /ā/: EI (vein, rein), EY (they, hey, prey, obey), EIGH (eight, weigh, sleigh, neighbour), AIGH (straight), EA (great, break, steak). Many of these words have homophones (rein/rain, weigh/way, great/grate) - discuss meanings.

bd.chain: vein → rein → reign → rain → rein → ray → prey → grey → hey → they → weigh → sleigh → neigh → eight → weight → freight → straight → great → break → steak

intro: We know many spellings of /ā/: a (baby), a_e (cake), ai (rain), ay (day). Today we will learn some less common spellings that appear in a few words.

115.tag: Alternate spellings of long U: ew, eu, ue /yū/ and ou /ū/
notes: EW and UE can spell /yū/ as well as /ū/: few, nephew, dew (/yū/) vs. new, blew (/ū/ in most Australian/NZ speech 'new' is /nyū/); cue, rescue, value (/yū/) vs. blue, glue (/ū/). EU spells /ū/ or /yū/ in a few words (neutral, feud). OU spells /ū/ in you, soup, group, youth.

intro: We know that EW, UI and UE spell /ū/ (new, fruit, blue), and that u_e can spell /ū/ or /yū/ (rule, cute). Today we will learn that EW and UE can also spell /yū/, the name of the letter U.

EW spells /yū/ in few, dew, nephew, curfew. UE spells /yū/ in cue, rescue, value, argue. EU is a rare spelling: neutral (/ū/), feud (/yū/). When you read ew or ue, try /ū/ and /yū/ to find the real word.
OU can also spell /ū/ in a few words: you, soup, group, youth. This is another sound for OU, which usually spells /ow/ (out).

117.title: Lesson 117 Signal Vowels
117.tag: Signal vowels: c /s/ and g /j/ before e, i, y
notes: E, I and Y are 'signal vowels': after C they signal /s/ (cent, city, cycle) and after G they usually signal /j/ (gem, giant, gym). Before A, O, U (and consonants) C spells /k/ and G spells /g/. Exceptions for G: get, give, girl, gift, begin.

bd.chain: cat → cent → city → cycle → cell → cellar → race → rice → ice → icy → mice → nice → gem → germ → gym → giant → gentle → magic → cage → page

intro: We have learned that C spells /k/ (cat) and /s/ in -ce (race), and that G spells /g/ (goat) and /j/ in -ge (cage). Today we will learn why.

The vowels E, I and Y are signal vowels. When C is followed by e, i or y, it signals the soft sound /s/: cent, city, cycle, cell. When G is followed by e, i or y, it usually signals /j/: gem, giant, gym, energy.
Before a, o, u or a consonant, C spells /k/ (cat, cot, cup, clap) and G spells /g/ (gap, got, gum, glad). A few common G words break the rule: get, give, girl, gift.

intro: Syllables are words or word parts with one vowel sound. Learning about syllables helps us read and spell.
Final stable syllables always come at the end of a word. We know one final stable syllable, -LE, as in apple and puzzle. Two more final stable syllables are -SION and -TION.

-sion: -SION can be pronounced two ways. When -SION follows a vowel (including r-controlled vowels), it is usually pronounced /zhən/ like in the words vision and diversion. When -SION follows a consonant letter, it is usually pronounced /shən/ like in the words passion and extension.
-tion: -TION can also be pronounced /shən/ like in the word fiction. -TION is sometimes pronounced /chən/ with TI making the /ch/ sound like in the word question.

We can break big words apart into syllables to help us read and spell. Display the word rotation. To read this word I can break it into syllables: ro - ta - tion, then blend the syllables together: rotation. As we read and spell, we can break words into syllables then blend them together.

121.title: Lesson 121 -er, -or, -ist
121.tag: The suffixes -er, -or and -ist mean some(one/thing) that does an action
notes: The focus of this lesson is on the meaning of the suffixes and their role in changing the part of speech. The concepts of nouns and verbs should be addressed separately, as needed.
In Lesson 100, students learned about the suffix -ER when used with adjectives to mean 'more than' (e.g., stronger). In this lesson, -ER is used to change verbs to nouns (e.g., teach → teacher).

bd.chain: read → reader → leader → lead → bead → beak → bake → baker → maker → taker → talker → walker

intro: Remember, a morpheme is a word part that changes a word's meaning. A suffix is a morpheme that comes at the end of a word. Today we will learn about three new suffixes: -ER, -OR, and -IST.

-er: We already know that when we add the suffix -ER to adjectives, it means more than like in the word bigger. When we add the suffix -ER to verbs, or action words, it makes the verb become a noun meaning one that does. Teach is a verb. Adding -ER to teach makes teacher. A teacher is a person who teaches. Print is a verb. Adding -ER makes printer. A printer is something that prints.

-or, -ist: -OR and -IST are also used to make verbs into nouns. -OR is pronounced /er/ (/ə/) as in sailor. -IST is pronounced /ist/ as in cartoonist. A sailor is someone who sails. A cartoonist is someone who draws cartoons.
Discuss how suffixes impact word meanings as you read and spell.

123.title: Lesson 123 -y
123.tag: The suffix -y means full of or described as
notes: Adding -y turns a noun into an adjective: cloud → cloudy (full of clouds). Spelling rules apply: 1-1-1 words double the consonant (sun → sunny, mud → muddy); silent e words drop the e (juice → juicy, shine → shiny).

intro: Suffixes are added to the end of a word to change the word's meaning. The suffix -Y means full of or described as. A cloudy day is full of clouds. A sleepy child is described as full of sleep.
When we add -Y to a 1-1-1 word, we double the last consonant: sun → sunny (the Double Consonant Rule). When we add -Y to a word that ends in silent e, we drop the e: juice → juicy (the Drop E Rule).
Adding -Y changes a naming word (noun) into a describing word (adjective): curl → curly, storm → stormy.

passage:
We all have good days and bad days. Good days are filled with brightness and happiness. On good days it is easy to be nice to our friends and everything seems fun. On good days annoying
things don’t really bother us, and we feel a sense of calmness in our bodies.

Bad days, on the other hand, are not so great. On bad days we may be filled with sadness or loneliness. Bad days can feel dark and scary. On bad days, it can be hard to be nice. On bad days lots of things might bother us, and we might not be in the mood for silliness.

When we are having a good day, we have the energy we need to spread kindness to the people around us. We can lend a smile or a helping hand and share our brightness with others. In return, when we are having a bad day, we can lean on those kindness spreaders for the extra help we need.
Because if everyone shares a little extra kindness on their good days, we can all help each other get through our bad days.

126.title: Lesson 126 -able, -ible
126.tag: The suffixes -able and -ible mean able or can do
notes: -able and -ible both mean 'able to be' or 'can be': washable (can be washed), flexible (able to flex). -able is usually added to whole base words (read → readable); -ible often attaches to Latin roots that are not whole words (visible, possible). Drop-e rule: observe → observable.

bd.chain: wash → washable → bend → bendable → teach → teachable → break → breakable → fix → fixable → flex → flexible → reverse → reversible → convert → convertible

intro: Suffixes are added to the end of a word to change the word's meaning. The suffixes -ABLE and -IBLE mean able or can do. Enjoyable means able to be enjoyed. Washable means it can be washed. Flexible means able to flex or bend.

-ABLE is usually added to a whole word: read → readable, wash → washable. When the base word ends in silent e, drop the e: observe → observable (the Drop E Rule). -IBLE is used with some word parts from Latin that are not whole words on their own: visible, possible, flexible.
Both suffixes sound the same: /əbəl/. When spelling, think about whether the base is a whole word (-able) or not (-ible).

passage: Cesar’s dog, Cooper, loves to play with toys. Chew toys are his favourite. The only problem is that Cooper treats his toys like they are disposable. You see, Cooper has super strong teeth and he likes to chew and tug on his toys until they are destroyed.

Cooper’s toys tend to last about a week. Once he pulled a toy apart in less than an hour! One day, Cesar brought home a gift for Cooper. “I think I finally found an indestructible dog toy,” he proclaimed. His family examined the toy. It was a set of three rubber rings linked together.

“These rings are extremely flexible and impossible to break,” Cesar explained. “They are washable so we can keep them clean. They even glow in the dark so they are visible at night!” Was it
possible? Was this finally the perfect toy for Cooper? Cooper loved his new rings and chewed on them every day.

Three months later, the rings had a few visible chew marks, but they were still useable. It was remarkable. This was the longest Cooper had ever kept a toy without tearing it apart. Cesar and his
family were all thrilled that they finally found an indestructible toy for their goofy, lovable pup.
tables: Something comfortable provides comfort, or lets you relax. A soft chair can be a comfortable place to sit.

127.title: Lesson 127 uni-, bi-, tri-
127.tag: The prefixes uni- (one), bi- (two) and tri- (three)
notes: These number prefixes come from Latin and Greek: uni- = one (unicorn, uniform), bi- = two (bicycle, bilingual), tri- = three (triangle, tricycle). Discuss the meaning of each word using the prefix.

bd.chain: cycle → unicycle → bicycle → tricycle → triangle → tripod → triplets → triple → bilingual → biweekly → uniform → unify → unicorn → universe

intro: Prefixes are added to the beginning of a word to change the word's meaning. Today we will learn three prefixes that tell us a number.

uni- means one. A uniform is one outfit that everyone wears. A unicycle has one wheel. bi- means two. A bicycle has two wheels. Bilingual means speaking two languages. tri- means three. A triangle has three angles. A tricycle has three wheels. Triplets are three babies born together.
When you see uni-, bi- or tri- at the beginning of a word, think about the number to help you understand the word.

passage:
Macy, Stacy, and Tracy are triplets. They do everything together. Each morning they wake up and put on matching uniforms. Then, they get on their bicycles and ride to school. At
school, they take all the same classes.

Their first class is French. The triplets are bilingual because they already speak English and Spanish. Once they learn French, they will be trilingual! Their next class is maths. In maths class, they learn all about different kinds of triangles. Then, in music class they practise a new song. They always sing in unison at the biweekly show.

After lunch, they go to reading class. This is the triplets’ favourite class. Their teacher is reading the last book in a new trilogy to them. They can not wait to learn how this story ends. At the end
of the day, the triplets get back on their bicycles and ride home together. They are an unbreakable trio.

128.title: Lesson 128 Affixes Review 2
notes: Review of the affixes from Lessons 121-127 plus earlier prefixes and suffixes. Word work: break words into parts and give definitions.

bd.chain: agree → agreement → disagreement → disagree → farm → farmer → farming → dark → darkness → darker → fix → fixable → fixer → happy → happiness → happier

intro: Morphemes are word parts that change what a word means. We have learned many suffixes: -er, -or and -ist (one that: teacher, sailor, artist), -ish (somewhat like: sluggish), -y (full of: cloudy), -ness (state of: kindness), -ment (result, act or state of: entertainment), -able and -ible (able to be: fixable, flexible). We have also learned the prefixes uni-, bi- and tri- (one, two, three).
To read a long word, find the prefix, the base word and the suffix. Read each part, then blend them and think about the meaning: dis-agree-ment, disagreement.

passage: The carnival is in town! Get your tickets, grab a friend, and head on down to the fairgrounds. With so many options for excitement and entertainment, everyone is bound to have a great day at the carnival.

If you are seeking adventure, head over to the sideshow alley. This is where you will find the rides. Slide down the bumpy slide, walk through the spooky haunted house, or buckle up for a ride on the
speedy roller coaster.
If you get hungry, wander over to the food trucks. Here you will find every imaginable treat. A giant hotdog, fairy floss, and an ice-cold lemonade are the perfect carnival combination.

If you get too hot and sweaty outside, step into the pavilion. Here you will meet farmers who can teach you about animals such as chickens, pigs and goats. You may even get to hold a baby chick! Also, there may be a cartoonist who will draw your caricature and a band playing music.
At the end of the day, everyone gathers to watch the firework display in the night sky. This part is never a disappointment. Spending the day at the carnival is always enjoyable.
